antispam.title: Anti-spam
antispam.desc: Inbound mail is scored at delivery (SPF, DKIM, DMARC, DNS blocklists, a Bayesian content model, and a SpamAssassin rule subset); a message over the threshold is filed to the recipient's Junk folder.
antispam.scoringDesc: The weight each signal adds to a message's spam score, and the thresholds it is measured against.
antispam.rulesetDesc: The rules contribute one combined signal to the spam score.
antispam.rulesHintA: Network-, plugin- and Bayes-backed rules, and patterns the engine cannot compile, are dropped; those checks are done natively.
antispam.rulesHintB: When the summed score of the rules reaches {0}, the verdict gains {1} points.
antispam.rulesHintC: The ruleset is seeded into data_dir on first run; refresh it with the antispam-rules tool, changes are applied automatically within about a minute, no restart.
antispam.bayesDesc: The content model that learns spam and ham from your users' mail.
antispam.greylistDesc: Defers the first message from an unknown sender, so only a server that retries gets through.
antispam.ratelimitDesc: Slows a flood of unauthenticated mail from one client network.
antispam.sizeDesc: The largest inbound message the server accepts.
antispam.outboundDesc: Caps how many external recipients one local account may send to within a window.
antispam.relayDesc: How a message that failed transiently is retried before it is returned to the sender.
antispam.gatewayDesc: Hands every outgoing message to one server instead of each recipient domain's mail exchangers.
antispam.digestDesc: A periodic summary of each user's new Junk mail, with a release link for every message.
antispam.autoreplyDesc: The subject an automatic reply falls back to when the mailbox stores none.
antispam.greylistHint: When on, the first message from an unknown sender (keyed by network, sender, and recipient) is deferred with a temporary failure so a legitimate server retries after a short delay; a spammer that does not retry never gets through. This delays first mail from new senders by a few minutes. Authenticated submission and allowlisted senders are never greylisted.
antispam.minDelayHint: Before a first-seen sender is accepted.
antispam.digestWarnB: is set in the server configuration, so
antispam.digestWarnStrong: no summary is sent at all
antispam.digestWarnC: , whatever this toggle says. Every entry carries a signed release link, so the digest cannot be built without the key. Set
antispam.digestWarnD: to the same value in the MTA and webmail configuration and restart the MTA.
antispam.digestHintA: When on, each user is emailed a periodic plain-text summary of newly quarantined (Junk) mail, every entry carrying a signed one-click link that releases that one message back to the inbox after a confirmation page. A per-mailbox watermark means only mail new since the last summary is included, and a mailbox with nothing new is skipped. The
antispam.digestHintB: is shared by the MTA, which signs the release links, and webmail, which verifies them.
antispam.autoreplyHint: An out-of-office reply is sent under the subject the user configured. EWS and ActiveSync carry no subject field, so a mailbox turned out of office from Outlook or a phone has none, and the reply uses this prefix followed by the subject of the message it answers. A mailbox that stores its own subject keeps it; this is only the fallback. Leave the field empty to restore the built-in wording.
antispam.relayHint: When delivery to a remote server fails transiently, the message is retried with an exponential backoff (the base delay below, doubling each attempt) until it succeeds or the attempt limit is reached, after which a non-delivery report is returned to the sender.
antispam.gatewayHint: Outgoing mail is normally delivered straight to each recipient domain's mail exchangers. With a gateway configured, every message is handed to that one server instead, which is what a network that blocks outbound port 25 requires. A domain can override this on its own page. MTA-STS, DANE and TLS reporting describe a recipient domain's own mail exchangers, so they do not apply to a gateway connection; the transport below is what protects it.
antispam.confirmRemoveGateway: Remove the outbound gateway? Mail is delivered directly to each recipient's mail exchangers again.
antispam.gwEnabled: Send outgoing mail through this gateway
antispam.gwPasswordStored: A password is stored; leave empty to keep it.
antispam.outboundHintA: When on, a local account that sends to more than the cap of external recipients within the window has the excess deferred with a temporary failure, a compromised account cannot blast spam unchecked, and an
antispam.outboundHintB: event is logged once per window so you can disable the account. Authenticated submission only; inbound mail is never affected.
antispam.sizeHint: The limit is advertised to senders as the SMTP SIZE extension. 0 means no limit; a larger message is rejected before it is queued.
antispam.ratelimitHint: When on, an unauthenticated client network (keyed by /24 or /64) that sends more than the burst within the window is deferred with a temporary failure, so a flood is slowed while a legitimate server simply retries. Authenticated submission is never rate limited.

antispam.modelColdStart: Using the built-in cold-start model. Retrain from your users' mail to improve it.
antispam.retrainHint: Retraining reads each mailbox's Junk folder as spam and inbox as ham; it runs in the background, watch the Task queue for the result.
antispam.scoringHint: Edited settings apply to inbound scoring within about a minute, no restart.

limits.title: Limits
limits.desc: Size, rate and connection limits for every protocol, and the login lockout. Each daemon applies a change within about a minute, no restart.
limits.sizeDesc: The largest request or body each protocol accepts; a larger one is rejected.
limits.rateDesc: Caps how many HTTP requests one client address may send within a window.
limits.connDesc: Caps the IMAP, POP3 and SMTP connections a daemon and one client address hold at once.
limits.lockoutDesc: Locks out an account and a client address after repeated failed logins.
limits.fetchDesc: Whether a fetchmail source may point at an internal address.
limits.commandLinesHint: A command line is one line a client sends before anything is stored, so these are in bytes, not megabytes. Without a cap a client that never ends its line grows the daemon's memory, and it reaches these readers before it logs in. Keep the IMAP figure generous: a long UID set or SEARCH is legitimate.
limits.ewsSubsHint: An EWS notification subscription is dropped once it goes unused for this long, so this is in minutes. The timer restarts every time the client uses the subscription, and it is the whole policy for a streaming subscription, whose request carries no timeout of its own. A client away for longer (a sleeping laptop, a roaming network) loses the subscription and cannot tell without subscribing again, so raise it when clients go offline for long stretches. A change applies to new subscriptions; existing ones keep the timeout they were created with.
limits.rateHint: When on, a client address that sends more than the burst within the window is answered with 429 and a Retry-After header, so one client cannot exhaust a daemon for everyone else. It covers every HTTP surface (webmail, EWS, ActiveSync, MAPI/HTTP, DAV, this panel and the gateway) and each daemon counts on its own. Keep the burst generous: Outlook and ActiveSync clients issue large legitimate bursts during an initial sync.
limits.connHintA: When on, a daemon serves at most the total number of connections at once, and one client address holds at most its own share. A refused connection is told why in the protocol's own greeting (IMAP
limits.connHintB: , which makes a sending server retry later rather than bounce the mail) and then closed. It covers IMAP, POP3 and SMTP; each daemon counts on its own. Keep the per-client figure generous: a desktop mail client holds several connections at once, and one address is often a whole office behind a NAT.
limits.lockoutHint: This is what makes online password guessing hopeless. It covers webmail, IMAP, POP3 and this panel; each daemon counts on its own, and every attempt counts twice: once against the account and once against the client address. The address is locked out at four times this threshold, since one address is often a whole office behind a NAT. Tighten it during a credential-stuffing wave, loosen it if legitimate users are being locked out. There is no off switch: raise the threshold instead.
limits.fetchHint: A fetchmail source is dialled by this server on a schedule, so a source pointed at an internal address reaches services that are not exposed to the network at all. Internal, loopback and link-local source addresses are therefore refused unless you allow them here. Turn this on only if you fetch from a server on your own private network. Domain administrators can create fetchmail entries; only a full system administrator can change this.

tls.title: TLS certificates
tls.desc: The certificate the gateway (front door) and the mail daemons present. An uploaded certificate overrides the config-file certificate and is picked up within about a minute, no restart.
tls.modeDesc: Serve uploaded certificates, or have the gateway obtain them from an ACME CA.
tls.modeHint: Manual serves the operator-uploaded certificates below. ACME has the gateway obtain and renew Let's Encrypt certificates automatically for every active domain's mail/autodiscover/autoconfig hosts (and the mta-sts host when publishing is on) over the TLS-ALPN-01 challenge, so each name must resolve to the gateway on :443. The apex is excluded, it is the domain owner's own website. A mode change takes effect when the gateway restarts; certificate contents still hot-reload without one.
tls.acmeAgree: I agree to the CA's terms of service
tls.storedDesc: Uploaded certificates by SNI name. Private keys are stored but never shown again.
tls.confirmDelete: Delete this certificate? Listeners fall back to the config-file certificate.
tls.none: No uploaded certificates, the listeners serve the config-file certificate.
tls.uploadDesc: Leave the name blank for the default certificate, or set an SNI host name to serve a specific host.
tls.mtastsDesc: Publish an MTA-STS policy (RFC 8461) so sending servers require validated TLS when delivering to this server.
tls.mtastsHintA: The gateway serves the policy at
tls.mtastsHintB: ; each domain's detail page then shows the
tls.mtastsHintC: and TLSRPT records its owner must publish. Testing mode reports TLS failures but still delivers; enforce mode makes senders refuse mail to a non-validated MX, so a certificate problem under enforce loses inbound mail. A change applies on the senders' next fetch, no restart.
tls.mtastsEnable: Publish an MTA-STS policy for hosted domains
tls.maxAgeHint: How long a sender caches the policy.
tls.enforceConfirm: I understand enforce can lose inbound mail if the MX certificate is invalid
tls.certsUnread: Could not read the stored certificates.
tls.acmeNoEmail: ACME mode needs an account email address.
tls.acmeNoAgree: ACME mode requires agreeing to the CA's terms of service.
tls.acmeNoURL: ACME mode needs an explicit CA directory URL. Leaving it blank would default to Let's Encrypt production and risk its rate limit on a misconfiguration; paste the production or staging directory URL.

tls.enforceNeedsConfirm: Enforce mode makes senders refuse mail when the MX certificate does not validate. Tick the confirmation box to enable it, or use testing mode first.

tls.mtastsSaved: Saved MTA-STS publishing. Publish each domain's prescribed mta-sts and _mta-sts records (see the domain page); senders adopt a change on their next fetch.

mailboxFailures.title: Mailbox failures
mailboxFailures.desc: Deliveries a recipient's own database refused for good.
mailboxFailures.notConfigured: Central logging is not configured, so these failures cannot be listed.
mailboxFailures.whatDesc: Nothing has bounced yet. Each message was deferred rather than rejected, so the sending server keeps retrying, and every retry fails the same way until the mailbox is repaired.
mailboxFailures.hintB: , which writes nothing and is safe on a running deployment. Repair it with
mailboxFailures.hintC: , which rebuilds a damaged database and loses the rows on its damaged pages. Repair refuses while a daemon holds the mailbox open.
